question: Consider the two functions \[ \begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^2+2bx+1,\\ g(x)&=2a(x+b), \end{aligned} \] where the variable \(x\) and the constants \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers. Each such pair of constants \(a\) and \(b\) may be considered as a point \((a,b)\) in an \(ab\)-plane. Let \(S\) be the set of such points \((a,b)\) for which the graphs of \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=g(x)\) do not intersect (in the \(xy\)-plane). The area of \(S\) is
solution:
An intersection requires the two functions to have the same value at some real \(x\). Setting \(f(x)=g(x)\) gives
\[
x^2+2(b-a)x+1-2ab=0.
\]
Completing the square reveals when this equation can have a real solution:
\[
(x+b-a)^2=a^2+b^2-1.
\]
As \(x\) ranges over the real numbers, the square on the left can equal any nonnegative number. Therefore an intersection exists exactly when \(a^2+b^2-1\ge0\). In particular, equality gives one intersection and must be excluded.

Thus the required parameter set is
\[
S=\{(a,b):a^2+b^2<1\}.
\]
This is the interior of the circle centered at the origin with radius 1. Its area is \(\pi\cdot1^2=\boxed{\pi}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The graphs intersect exactly when the equation \(f(x)=g(x)\) has a real solution. Rearranging it gives
\[
x^2+2(b-a)x+1-2ab=0.
\]
Its leading coefficient is always 1, so it is a quadratic for every pair \((a,b)\). Its discriminant is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta
&=[2(b-a)]^2-4(1-2ab)\\
&=4(a^2+b^2-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
A quadratic has no real roots exactly when its discriminant is negative. Hence the graphs do not intersect precisely when
\[
a^2+b^2<1.
\]
The boundary \(a^2+b^2=1\) gives a repeated real root, so it is excluded. The resulting region is the open disk of radius 1, with area \(\boxed{\pi}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Use the discriminant
